utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. And out there in New York. I guess it's good morning to you. Madam Registrar will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances for today, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. It's Carmela Javier, Lorna Bolton, and Mark Harmon for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Kay Marshall, Novak Lukic, and I'm Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith, on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Good morning once again, Mr. Sacirbey. May I just remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I understand that Mr. Guirguis had asked if he could be excused for day; and in his place if Ms. Corominas, the other counsel who attended yesterday, could sit in on today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess we had agreed on that yesterday, yeah. I think we can get a replacement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guirguis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: I will be replaced by Ms. Corominas for the remainder of the examination and I will return for the cross-examination, with the court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we could please get the name of new counsel on record.

utterances.speaker: MS. COROMINAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Annemarie Corominas, counsel for Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could start off where we left off yesterday, which was at Resolution 771, which you will find in tab 9 of the 1992 binder, and it should be --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And for the Court, this is 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is a resolution, sir, dated -- from the Security Council dated August 13th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And are you familiar with this resolution, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The third paragraph on the first page reads as follows: "Expressing grave alarm at continuing reports of widespread violations of international humanitarian law occurring within the territory of the former Yugoslavia and especially in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including reports of mass forcible expulsion and deportation of civilians; imprisonment, and abuse of civilians in detention centre; deliberate attacks on non-combatants, hospitals, and ambulances; impeding the delivery of food and medical supplies to the civilian population; and wanton devastation and destruction of property." We have already touched a bit on events from 1992 yesterday, but just for clarification the reference to the reports of mass forcible expulsion and deportation of civilians, imprisonment and abuse of civilians in detention centres, what events are those -- were those being referenced to in the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was originally a report from the Secretary-General that actually referred to such events as ethnic purification. By this point in time we started, in fact, identifying them under the term "ethnic cleansing" and this refers, of course, to the expulsion of people from their homes or sometimes the murder of people, that is, large groups of people. It also refers to what we have sometimes called "elite-icide" [phoen] which is actually that -- that is the leaders of societies of towns, of urban centres were usually murdered in some ways in very public fashion while others were in fact forced from their homes with what we believe was the notion to scare them to such a degree that those people would never want to return to their homes. In addition to that, cultural centres religious centres, were in fact destroyed so that those people could not return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. What you've just been describing --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I may. If the Chamber could direct the witness to use the personal pronoun of "I" as opposed to the plural pronoun of "we," I think it might be of some assistance to the record, because we're talking about a variety of different subjects. And yesterday he oftentimes used the word "we" as opposed to "I" and -- unless he can -- If we could have some kind of clarity as to when he's making these presentations whether he's speaking a collective position, a position that he is taking on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or whether is he talking about something which is specific unto himself. I think it would be of some assistance to the record as it stands, because of the fact that we are now also dealing with Security Council resolutions and reports. So when one says, We believe, the "we" is unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's fine, I will clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: First of all, sir, when you were talking or using the word "we" in answer to the question I just asked, on whose behalf were you speaking?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case I was speaking on behalf of the mission of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the United Nations, of which I was the permanent representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My original question had been about -- what I wanted to understand is what historical events were being referenced when we were talking about the reports of mass forcible expulsion, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: These events related to what we had already received reports on. Generally initially the reports were mostly from the Drina river valley. By this time we also had reports from what is called the Krajina region of Bosnia which in particular includes the town of Prijedor which we believe suffered at that time almost 30.000 dead and was entirely ethnically cleansed of its non-Serb population. It also refers to the suburbs of Sarajevo which fell under the control of the Serbian forces, including -- particularly the suburb of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, there was a request that you replace the preposition "we" with -- the pronoun "we," rather, with either the BiH mission, or "I," if you are talking in the singular, if you're talking about yourself; and if you're talking about the mission, say the BiH embassy or whatever it's was called. I don't know what it was called.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will reference that in the future to the BiH mission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The -- if I could refer you to the same page of this resolution sir, to numbered paragraph number 2?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We see there the use of the term "ethnic cleansing?"

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Had that term been used in any UN resolution prior to this date?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm actually not aware of it being used. As I said, there was Secretary-General's report before that that referred to ethnic purification. I believe that this is the first official use of that term in a UN Security Council resolution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was there a discussion or agreement in the Security Council as to what kinds of activities that word would encompass or what that -- the definition of that term was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This term was interpreted by some as equating to "genocide." By others it was equated to as "acts of genocide."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- I'm going to interrupt. I'm not interested in how it was interpreted. My question was: Was there discussion or agreement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was discussion on that term.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Was there agreement on what it meant?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily to the precise -- to the precise degree.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. In the discussion that took place, what kinds of activities were contemplated or discussed as falling within that rubric?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly the expulsion of the population. Certainly the murder of individuals, and groups of individuals. "Elite-icide." The destruction of cultural and religious properties. The type of activities that somehow would compel that population, would instill terror into them not to want to return to their homes. That was generally agreed to. The -- probably the major difference was one of whether this was absolutely systematic and would be equated to genocide, or whether it was something that was an act of genocide. That was the general distinction maybe that existed in some countries' views.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. There is an reference in this document to deliberate attacks on non-combatants, hospitals, an ambulances. And that's in the paragraph that I've already read to you. I'm wondering if those references relate to any historic events in particular.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They occurred throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina from places like Mostar, to Sarajevo, to other areas. They were most well documented by media and other sources though in Sarajevo, and there was significant evidence of civilians -- clearly civilians being targeted; those civilians then being wounded or murdered; and those who would come to assist them, including medical personnel being targeted. There was also attacks on hospitals, including the hospitals in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to turn to a different topic now. Could you tell me -- the topic I'm going to be discussing with you, sir, are the reports of the Special Rapporteur of the United Nations -- the UNHCR. Human Rights Commission? HRC? Do you ...

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a United Nations Human -- well there's a -- there's a UN -- are you looking for my answer, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am. Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's, of course, the United Nations Human Rights Commission, and there's also the United Nations Refugee Agency. I believe you're talking about United Nations Human Rights Commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. I neglected to ask that that last document we were discussing be marked as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2438.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What is the mandate of the United Nations Human Rights Commission?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can, of course, be defined by the moment, but it is generally to address human rights issues, those that are consistent with standards of the international community, that is, the United Nations. It may, in fact, in instances then appoint Special Rapporteurs to view a particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what relationship does it have, if any, to the United Nations General Assembly or the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such reports then may be issued for review by the General Assembly and/or Security Council, and they recommend that further measures be taken by either one of those bodies. Probably more likely than not the UN Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a series of reports that were authored by a man named Tadeusz Mazowiecki during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was his post?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was, in fact, appointed as a Special Rapporteur to study the violations or - let me be more accuracy on that - the situation of grave violations of international humanitarian law in the former Yugoslavia, particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just for clarification, who would have appointed him as Special Rapporteur?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: United Nations Human Rights Commission. He may have been nominated by -- or he may have in fact selected as a potential Special Rapporteur by some other third party, but in fact it would be -- he would be accountable to the United Nations Human Rights Commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And where did he have his business offices, or office?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- excuse me. The United Nations Human Rights Commission is actually headquartered out of Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you know him prior to his appointment?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I knew of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What was his background?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a former official in the post-communist government of Poland.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you ever have a friendship or personal relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had never met him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And with respect to his reports, I would you to turn to tab 10 of the binder in front of you. And what I'd like you to do is -- we're going to go through each tab very quickly and just have you look at the document and confirm for me whether it is, in fact, a report that he authored, okay? So the first tab --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- is tab 10A. And you should have before you 65 ter 5701 report dated 28th of August, 1992. Do you see that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I should indicate, sir, that sometimes we've reproduced the entire document, and sometimes we have reproduced only a portion of it. Do you recognise whether this is a true copy of the report that was authored by the Special Rapporteur?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do. And it does certainly appear to be an authentic copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are these reports, sir, that -- sorry. Are these reports, sir, that you would have read in your capacity as the ambassador?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and we may have recommended that, of course, they be adopted as documents by the other United Nations agencies, institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that document could be admitted as an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this may well be a document that was covered in your decision on application of Rule 73 bis an amendment of indictment dated the 15th of May, 2007, specifically footnote number 16. Without further guidance from the Prosecution as to the ostensible purpose of the use of this document, I would have to object at this time based upon the ruling found in -- in that decision. But if I have further understanding of what the Prosecution's purpose is in seeking to admit this particular report, I may not be objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know what those decisions mean. Maybe you do. Can you respond?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't have a copy of the decision or the footnote that my friend's referring to at -- perhaps he could enlighten us as to what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This deals with the issue of leading a particular kind of evidence that we've discussed before, and I'm hesitant to mention that particular kind of evidence in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given the particular situation we find ourselves in, do you mind walking across to find out what it is all about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't mind sharing with the Prosecution at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We may need a minute or two, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised that if there is any need for further discussion of the document without the witness hearing, the Registrar in New York can press the mute button and we can talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, there's not. We have resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll just put on record that the Prosecution does not intend to rely on the document for the prohibited purpose that is set out in the document. We intend to rely on it for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's understood. With regard to the specific footnote and concerns that were made by the -- by this Chamber with regard to that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then you may proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. If it could be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. For the limited purposes that it is being tendered for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I raise another concern about all of these documents. Which is that to the extent that these documents contain within them unsourced hearsay information. If they're being offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted, we interpose an objection at this time. With regard to all of the documents that were produced by this particular gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Naturally, the Chamber is not in possession of that decision or doesn't even have an idea of what kind of documents these are. We will rely on you to remind us each time such kind of document comes up. The document is admitted into evidence, for that limited purpose. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2439.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, maybe I will just ask you to take a few moments so we don't go through each tab individually. If you could take a few moments and just look at the documents in each of the tab. And if you can, the question I will be asking you after you have done that is if your satisfied that these are true copies of the reports that Mr. -- that were released by the Special Rapporteur during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interject, Madam Bolton. You want to share with the Chamber the purpose for which they are now being tendered. If they're not tendered for the truthfulness of their contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: They're being tendered as a notice of the allegations that were being made against the Bosnian Serb forces at the time, which would then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whether or not those allegations are true.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's a separate issue as to whether they're true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You may then proceed, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just waiting for the witness to finish his global review of the tabs. It will probably just take him another minute or to two, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a relatively large binder, so it's going to take a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yeah, I'm trying to make sure I'm complete because I'm looking at the areas the reports cover because I was aware of those, and they have covered a large area. I was also just very briefly making sure that I took a look at the source for the report which was also relevant, and I did see that as well. So at least from the first few documents, I'm quite comfortable that these are authentic. I will now go through the rest of them, and, just to be absolutely complete, I will let you know once I have had an opportunity to read them all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the one that is very extensive here. The last report that I believe I'm at is one 21 February 1994. It is the sixth periodic report. The documents seem to go into something else at that point in time. Am I accurate?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There may be a tab that contains two reports, and I'll need your assistance with that. There may also be a second report in that tab, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In tab -- which letter? I'm in tab E right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In tab E you should have 65 ter 5699, report from 5th May 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I have -- oh from 1993, that would have been a previous tab then. I'm sorry, I'm looking at the wrong -- the document at the top is labelled E, but in fact it is tab G, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Just for the purposes of the record, Your Honours, that is 65 ter 02058.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: For tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So we don't go through this kind of confusion because we unfortunately are like the Chamber, we don't have the tabbed documents the same way that the Prosecution and the witness does. If we go through the exercise that the witness is going through right now, which is reviewing the documents and confirming his position about them, then I think we should start at the beginning and go through each tab so we know specifically which 65 ter number it is, what tab is attributed to it, and then they can move for its admission in whatever fashion they wish to do. I think it might be a little simpler than doing something halfway through.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. I do intend to clarify what's in each tab, and I can do it that way. I was hoping to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: But let's go through, sir, each tab just to confirm what's in it, okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So we have already dealt with tab A. Could you go to stab B, please, which is 10B and you should have 65 ter 5700.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And that's got a date of 27th October 1992 on it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you have reviewed that report. You have reviewed that tab?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And are you satisfied that that is a true copy of Mr. Mazowiecki's original report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be tendered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the -- this exhibit and all further exhibits, so I don't have to rise each time and take up more time. It's my understanding that the Prosecution's position remains the same as the reasons for which these particular reports are being tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If my friend means by "all future exhibits" the Special Rapporteurs reports, then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I certainly wouldn't mean the thousands of exhibits that exist in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do you confirm?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I do, yes, with respect to the Mazowiecki and Special Rapporteur report, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Then 65 ter 5700 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2440.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you look at tab C, please, sir, and you should have 65 ter 2168. It should be a --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- report dated 17 November 1992 from the Special Rapporteur?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that it's a true copy of the original report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. This report speaks of the fear, ultimate goal of a Greater Serbia. I remember this one quite well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2441, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you turn to tab D, please, sir. You should have 65 ter 2167 which is a report dated the 10th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And is that the document in that tab?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just had a chance to look at it before, briefly. That is -- I believe this is also authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could it be introduced as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you turn to tab E, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You should have a report, 65 ter 5699, with a date of 5th May 1993 on it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And, again, are you satisfied that that's a true copy of the original report issued by the Special Rapporteur?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. This deals with the Drina river valley, particularly Srebrenica. I'm familiar with this one as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2443, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Turn to tab F, you may have more than one document in tab F; I'm not sure. If you could look at 65 ter 2059, report dated 26 August 1993, the third periodic report. Do you have that document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And I remember this one again because it speaks of the use of basic utilities as a weapon of war. That had become a particular problem at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And is that report only nine pages in length?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, two, three, four -- yes, it is. It is -- yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And is there another document in that same tab behind it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- no these are translations, excuse me. No, there is not. The next tab is tap G which is 21 February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. That's where your binder and my binder are going to differ.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So let's just ask first that the document we've just been discussing be marked as exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 2059 is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2444, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So you say the next document that you have is a report dated what date?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: 21st February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Registrar, will be looking to see if anything has been misplaced, but I don't think so, Madam Bolton. At least not here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. So exhibit -- or tab G you have a document, 65 ter 2058; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And that document, in my copy, is pages 1 to 20 only of that report. Does that correspond with your copy?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I remember this by one of the front titles which is terrorisation of Muslims and Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Serb-held territory which was then becoming a big issue at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just for your information, sir, we aren't going to be discussing acts of terror in these proceedings, okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just reading the title of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you satisfied that that is an excerpt of a -- or a true copy of a portion of that report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it please be so marked. It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P2445, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking at tab H Sir, you should have -- 10H, of course, 65 ter 2114.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we -- wait a second. Oh, yes, I do have it. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And that's dated the 4th of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And it's a 60-page document? If you would just flip to the back.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And again can you confirm whether that's a true copy of the report issued by the Special Rapporteur?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This one -- again, a few familiar headings, including the situation of detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2446, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The next tab, sir, tab IJ should be a report with a 65 ter number of 5009 dated 16 January 1995. And that's a 31-page report, with annexes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And again can you confirm whether that's a true copy of the report issued by Mr. Mazowiecki?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That could be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2447, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Turning to tab K, sir, 10K. You should have a report, 65 ter 2061, dated the 5th of July, 1995, and that is a report, 32 pages.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this report. I'd just like to point out that, at this date, I had also assumed the post of the foreign minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you continue to review Mr. Mazowiecki's reports after you assumed that post?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And I continued to hold a title of permanent representative. At that time the mission was also directed at -- in my absence by my deputy, i.e., charge d'affaires.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at the next tab, 10L, please. You should have a report -- the 65 ter 5711.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go to that one, what do you with 2061?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be tendered, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is submitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will become Exhibit P2448, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And what is the next 65 ter, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: 5711, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That should be a document with the date of 22nd August 1995, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm again very familiar with this report, as it was something that was part of my responsibility as foreign minister, and I should also add, as the agent for Bosnia-Herzegovina before the International Court of Justice, so I had several reasons to review these reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And just -- if I could ask you to turn to page 26 of this report. Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Annex 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. What is that document in Annex 1?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is A letter from Mr. Mazowiecki to the Chamber on the Commission of Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what's the gist of the letter; do you recall it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is a point in time when Mr. Mazowiecki was critical of the fact that his reports had received inadequate action, and he was at the point of resigning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that document be marked as an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In particular I should add that there is an emphasise here, of course, of what happened in Srebrenica and Zepa which had occurred during that summer and was viewed as an unfortunate, obviously lapse in -- in view of all the other previous reports that in fact Srebrenica and Zepa had been allowed to happen by whatever reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2449, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the last tab you should have under 10 is tab 10M, and that's a 65 ter 5010. And you should have a report dated 7 November 1995. And this report was authored by Elisabeth Rehn who was the new Special Rapporteur. Do you have that report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And again is this a true copy of her report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please note at that time we were in Dayton involved in negotiations and this one might be just a little more ... -- yes, it is a true report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be tendered as a document, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P2450, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, sir, to turn back to tab 10A.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have to --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And that is now exhibit P2439.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, I was having trouble hearing you in that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry that was for the court's assistance. Just giving them the exhibit number, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, we're there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could ask you to turn to paragraph 1 of the actual text of the report.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would this be under the title "Introduction."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 purports to set out the task that he was given. It indicates that his being appointed the Commission of Human Rights adopted resolution on the 14th August 1992 to appoint a Special Rapporteur and then I'll quote: "To investigate firsthand the human rights situation and the territory of the former Yugoslavia in particular within Bosnia and Herzegovina; and to receive relevant and credible information on the human rights situation there from governments, individuals, intergovernmental and non-governmental organisations on a continuing basis and to avail him or herself -- himself or herself of the assistance of existing mechanisms of the commission on human rights." My question for you, sir, is: Did the government or the mission of Bosnia-Herzegovina provide any information to the Special Rapporteur in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we did. But it was minimum. Most of the information that was provided to the rapporteur was one that was received on the ground. The Special Rapporteur frequently was actually in the territory firsthand reviewing these facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And apart from the minimal information you provided to the Special Rapporteur, did you or anyone associated with your government -- were you involved in any way in the preparation of Mr. Mazowiecki's reports?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly was not, and -- nor am I aware that anyone from my mission. Was and I have never heard of anyone from the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina involved in authoring the reports. Undoubtedly there were individuals who were sources for information.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you or anyone in your mission have any -- or in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the best of your knowledge have any influence over what reports of abuse he investigated?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No we did not. At least I don't believe we did, unless Mr. Mazowiecki, on his own or his staff chose to review submissions that we had made to the Secretary-General, or to the General Assembly, or to the Security Council, or to the Internation Court of Justice and then basically use those submissions as a beginning source to further evaluate the situation. That could have happened. But I'm not particularly aware of any pattern of conduct in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was anyone in your mission or your government, to the best of your knowledge, involved in authoring or influencing any of the conclusions or recommendations he made in his reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Objection. Compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was anyone involved, to the best of your knowledge, in influencing any of the conclusions that he reached in his reports?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how about the recommendations that he made?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certainly not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you comment on how -- or to whom -- Mr. -- First, how were Mr. Mazowiecki's reports released?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were released as documents generally of ECOSOC and the Human Rights Commission; but then at various points in time, they may have been made also documents of the General Assembly and/or Security Council. They may have been also issued as part of the Secretary-General's reports. At various times, countries may have also made a particular allusion to certain elements of these reports in providing further communication to the Security Council and to the -- and to the General Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I missed the acronym that the gentleman used and apparently so did the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I also missed it. I heard --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Economic and Social -- Economic and Social Council, Your Honour, of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall whether these reports were ones that you had to -- your mission had to actively seek out, or were they circulated to you as a matter of course?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we would not have to seek them out. They were circulated as a matter of course. Certainly if it's circulated by the Economic and Social Council and the Human Rights Commission, it would be circulated to the entire membership of the United Nations, including, in this case, the FRY, which was in fact privy to such circulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were any of these reports discussed in the United Nations Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extensively and certainly to the extent that we felt that they were relevant to the considerations of Security Council, we, on numerous occasions made emphasis to them, because obviously they were indicating a rather grave situation consistent with the Security Council's mandate to address both the threat to international peace and security but also to the threat -- to the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey by "we" once again you mean the Bosnia and Herzegovina mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina. Yes I thought I was a little more precise, but I will endeavour again, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I lost my train of thought for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Please don't do that, Your Honour. Just having a little brain freeze for a moment. Sorry I have lost whatever thought I had. So I will move on. Oh, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I remember now. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were any of his reports referenced in any of the resolutions adopted by the United Nations Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do believe they were. And certainly they were referenced by consideration. What I mean by that, if not referenced by an action paragraph, they were referenced by the fact that they were a basis for the Security Council's actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. You've indicated that you have, at some point in time, read the documents that are in tabs 10A to M. If you read nothing about the conflict other than the reports of the Special Rapporteur, would you have been aware of the fact that there were allegations being levelled against the Serb forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina of targeting civilians in Sarajevo with shell and sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly. I believe the reports are even more extensive than the media reports that were available at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Would have you known that accusations were being levelled that the Serbian forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina were engaging in acts of ethnic cleansing including rape, summary executions, and forcible transfers?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Objection, leading. At this point, it's leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is that are you leading, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kinds of issues -- you've told us what the mandate of the Special Rapporteur's reports were. Can you tell us what kinds of issues he discussed in terms of any allegations that were being levelled against the Bosnian Serb forces in his reports?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I only fear that I may leave something out. But I believe it was very comprehensive review that addressed matters of not only physical harm to the population; that is, murder, rape, forced deportation. But it was also one of denial of access to water and basic necessities of like, medicine. It was one also that spoke of the destruction of cultural and religious sites. And then the continued punishment, if you would, I'm trying to avoid using a certain word. Let me use the word trying to scare the population off that remained in some of these areas controlled by the Serbian forces. So we have from one end of actual physical harm being inflicted to the point of death and murder; another one, to the point that people were in fact being detained in camps, concentration camps, detention camps, whichever term you prefer; to the point of where individuals being denied access to necessities of life, food, water, utilities; and besieged, not being allowed to obviously move freely. And as I mentioned even in those who were by some chance left under the territories that were at that time occupied that their life continued to be made very difficult so that they would in fact abandon their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I just have a couple more questions, and then it's going to be time for the break, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could have a two-minute indulgence, Your Honour. Is that all right, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have two minutes without indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, was there any discussions to the best of your recollection in the reports authored by the Special Rapporteur as to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes there was. Of course, all the acts that I had mentioned to you would be violations of the Geneva Conventions as well as actually at this time what -- what is relevant to us, of course, relevant to the UN Security Council resolutions, which referenced the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you -- when you expressed an opinion there, that they would be violations of the Geneva Conventions, the acts that you have described, whose -- whose conclusion was that? Is that your personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, no. I was saying that the resolutions would, in fact, reference those. So they would be, of course, a reference in the Mazowiecki report. And there would also a reference, therefore, in the UN Security Council decisions or presidential statements -- most of UN resolutions of that -- UN Security Council resolutions at that time were under chapter 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any reason to believe that representatives of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia' mission at the United Nations ever read the Special Rapporteur's reports?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. There was discussion on these points. There was a discussion regarding the specifics. There were some responses. And certainly they were present there when these matters were addressed either particularly within the Security Council or other bodies of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What do you mean -- sorry, I should pause. What do you mean by responses?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they were informal responses. At some point in time there may have also been submitted responses in writing that were either explicit or implicit to the points outlined in the Mazowiecki report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And these are --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. Three's are responses --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to make a considerable pause between question and answer for the benefit of the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: These are responses, sir, being either written or orally coming from whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like -- that question is compound. Written responses or oral responses. We need to break them down so we know what we're referring to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, any response to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The oral responses you were referring to, from whom would they come?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, of course, like to be more precise. First of all, at that time I was involved also in negotiations regarding the situation in Bosnia. So these issues were also brought up during the negotiations that I was involved in at various sites from Geneva to New York, to other places. And number 2 we also brought these issues up in our case of which I was agent - that is, our case, that is the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina versus Serbia and Montenegro brought before the Internation Court of Justice. In all of these instances as well as in my capacity as ambassador, that is, permanent representative of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the United Nations - I'll try to slow down for the translator. We brought these matters up either directly or indirectly, and these matters were responded to by the representatives in each one of those capacities, that is either the council on behalf of the FRY before the Internation Court of Justice, the negotiators on behalf of the FRY during the negotiations, or the permanent mission of the FRY Serbia and Montenegro to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It is break time, Mr. Sacirbey, and we will come back to this issue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We take a break and come back at 4.00 p.m. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, before the break, you had mentioned in response to a question I asked you about how you knew that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had read -- or that that their mission had read the report. You mentioned there were responses, and you mentioned some of them were written. Who made written responses to the Special Rapporteur's reports?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least I'm familiar with a couple of instances where the representatives of the mission of the FRY, that is Serbia and Montenegro to the United Nations, had responded. And I believe those responses were to the Security Council, or to the president of the Security Council, more accurately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was there any coverage of the Special Rapporteur's reports in the media?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in the media that I was familiar with, yes. Quite extensive, in the region and in international media.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we look at portions of exhibit -- sorry, of tab 10A for you. And it's exhibit 2439, Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm there, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. This is the first of the Special Rapporteur's reports, I believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if I could -- I'm going to turn your attention to a few passages, and then I will have some questions for you, okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could ask you to turn to numbered paragraphs 6 and 7. Have you found those passages, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 indicates: "Most of the territory of the former Yugoslavia, in particular Bosnia and Herzegovina, is, at present the scene of massive and systematic violations of human rights, as well as serious grave violences of humanitarian law. Ethnic cleansing is the cause of most such violations." Paragraph 7 continues: "The Special Rapporteur was able to collect credible testimony concerning the policy of ethnic cleansing and the methods applied to achieve its aim. According to the testimony received, the policy has been openly pursued on the territory of those parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia which are controlled by ethnic Serbs." Were those sections or comments by the Special Rapporteur the subject of any inform or formal discussions at the UN Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, the question is compound. And I think there needs to be a distinction between that which is informal and that which is formal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Again, it's up to me if I feel there needs to be clarification, Your Honour, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. Compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My response is the same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Will you please repeat it just for the sake of clarity?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, is there any discussion of the -- these sections of the report in informal consultations of the Security Council, to which you were privy?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How much was it discussed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extensively.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you recall whether or not there was a discussion in any of the formal sessions of the Security Council, the public sessions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What significance did your government, if any, attach to these comments?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly they spoke of particular facts that constituted grave violations of humanitarian law. It, in fact, gave now new meaning -- I shouldn't say new meaning. It confirmed the notion of ethnic cleansing and what it constituted and, of course, it spoke of these violations being committed in the area controlled by, as it cites here, ethnic Serbs. We frankly would use the word "Serbian forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By which you would mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we always understood that this term, "Serbian forces" referred to the forces of Belgrade, the military force of Belgrade, as well as those, in fact, that were their agents in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I say "we," that is, the mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina to be again very clear on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And if you had to distinguish between those two, what terminology would you use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would refer maybe to the term "Pale Serbs." We were -- "we," again, the mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I believe the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina with its multi-ethnic makeup, was committed to preserving a multi-cultural, multi-ethnic state; and therefore we did not wish to see any of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina be somehow branded in any fashion by its ethnicity. We only wished to see political or ideological forces be branded for their actions within Bosnia and Herzegovina. While victims may have been identified by their religion or ethnicity, we did not wish to identify perpetrators by such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in this specific incident when you said "Serbian forces" you meant both the Pale forces and the Serbian forces as in Serbia, or did you mean either of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We met both because it was "we," again, the mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honour it was difficult sometimes for us to distinguish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew there was a free movement of goods and, of course, men across the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: One of the phrases that the Special Rapporteur used is the phrase "systematic violations." Did that have any interest to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Systematic violations would now go beyond individual acts that may have been perpetrated, let's say in a moment of particular military action or one might even say in the heat of the movement. In fact, these actions were not coincidental to the conflict, but in fact were the very purpose. These actions were intended to drive the population. So we -- if we want to discuss gender-based crimes, of course, there was also rape of men. But rape of women, enforced pregnancy; they were intended to in fact derive a result of genocide. So this was not just a coincidental measure or element of the war; in fact, it was the intended purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you're speaking there, again, are you expressing your personal views, or those of your government, or someone?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm actually expressing there the views -- and particular, of course, the mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because we had an opportunity to evaluate this information and try to address it in the context of our responsibilities vis-a-vis various institutions of the international community. I also actually -- that context could address it in terms of our efforts before the Internation Court of Justice, as I said, while I was an agent, I could also address that in the context of negotiation where I was one of the negotiators on behalf of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So it was actually in all of those capacities.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you turn to paragraph 17 and 18 of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I just have you confirm for me what is being discussed in paragraphs 17 and 18.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are speaking here of the siege, as -- as it very much focuses now also on tactics that are intended, or strategy if you would really, that are intended to deprive the population of essential goods, but also obviously the tactic of directly inflicting harm, that is, through shelling and sniping. Paragraph 18 brings us to this term and -- that I would, of course, I would uses a different term in today's world, but it is one that is meant to threaten and scare the population --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I'm going to cut you off there, okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't want to discuss that issue. And, again, did you have any -- anyone from your mission or you personally have any influence on the conclusions that the Special Rapporteur reaches in paragraph 17, for example, that -- sorry, that snipers, for example, shoot innocent civilians?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. Not that I'm aware of, any way, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you turn to just the last section of the report which is the recommendations section, and it starts at page -- sorry, at paragraphs 58 and following.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: One of the recommendations made in this document is that a commission be established to investigate specific cases and determine whether prosecution is warranted. Do you recall that recommendation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was that acted upon?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: UN Security Council resolution way adopted which then established a commission of experts which in fact then brought about the birth of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, and our mission to the United Nations strongly endorsed all of those steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And if I could just ask you in that regard. You mentioned two things: The commission of experts, and the establishment of the Tribunal. Could you turn to tab 11, please. This is it 65 ter 6572.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we there? We're just having a little difficulty getting through the papers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I don't what is worse electronics or binders.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Resolution 780?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, tab 11 is not that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the resolution number?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Resolution 780. Should be --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have Resolution 781 in front of me. And tab 80 is a different document. Let me see if I can help. I do not have Resolution 780 at least in that location. But I'm sure if you wish me to speak about it, I am familiar with those.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. We have it in electronic form. Let me just read you the -- the -- well, first, do you recall what that accomplished, Resolution 780?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I believe -- if I'm -- Ms. Bolton, I would prefer that you always give me the subject matter so that I'm just not -- this was the time, of course, that we did have the -- the UN resolution adopted regarding the commission of experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't want you to guess. Let me -- I will read you the pertinent passage. I'm reading to you, sir, from Resolution 780 paragraph 2, document reads: "Request the Secretary-General to establish as a matter of urgency an impartial commission of experts to examine and analyse the information submitted pursuant to Resolution 771, 1992, and the present resolution together with such further information as the commission of experts may obtain through its own investigations or efforts of other persons or bodies pursuant to Resolution 771 with a view to providing the Secretary-General with its own conclusions on the evidence of grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and other violations of international humanitarian law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia." Now that I have read that passage to you, sir, does that refresh your memory as to what Resolution 780 achieved?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes it does. It was also a particular point of discussion during the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What did Resolution 780 achieve, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the first step in evaluating the methodology by which an international crime Tribunal would be established. And also the commission of experts did in fact bring about a lot of documentary and other evidence regarding the types of violations of international humanitarian law that were happening on the territory. I actually reviewed a lot of that evidence personally, and it did leave an impact upon me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did the -- was a commission of experts in fact established?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that 65 ter -- that the document we've been discussing, 65 ter 6572 be marked as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is submitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2451, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just -- the binder that you were just looking at, sir, did it have a --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- label on it of a year? Because it should have been in a binder marked "1993."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, okay. Well, we were looking at a binder called -- labelled "1992." And that's where tab 11 was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Just take a moment, if you wouldn't mind, just turn to tab 11 in that binder number 2 to see if is in fact there. Resolution 780?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I see what you're saying. I did not understand your comment. No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's not in the 1993 binder?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, 1992 we were looking at. I'm sorry, there is no -- is there a tab 11?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The 1993/1994 binder, Your Honours, starts at tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. All right. If you would give Mr. Sacirbey the tab 14, the binder 1993. And if you would turn to tab 14. The other issue we were discussing was -- you mentioned the establishment of the Tribunal. And you should have at tab 14 Resolution -- 65 ter number 4928. Which is Resolution 808.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And there, there is a reference on the first page in the last paragraph to the Security Council having considered an interim report of the commission of experts. And the commission --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "And the commission having observed that the decision to establish an ad hoc international Tribunal in relation to events in the territory of the former Yugoslavia would be consistent with ... its work." And then on the next page, it would appear there was a decision to establish an international Tribunal. Is that a fair summary of what this resolution accomplished, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2452.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, madam. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if could you turn in that 1993 binder, sir, to tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will this be also within 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We may be having a little difficulty again identifying this document. Could you identify the resolution number? Maybe we can find it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Resolution 827.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We have tab 15.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We don't have tab 16 here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I was able to read the screen before, so maybe we could employ that method again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Oh all right. You were able to see it electronically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at it electronically then if that's working for us.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So the 65 ter number is 5001. And the -- Madam Registrar is going to display it for you, I think.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I can make it out pretty well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. And how did -- sorry, this is also a resolution that discusses --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were able to now find tab 16 in another book, and it, as you mentioned, Resolution 827. So we can go back to whatever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Properly easier for you to read the paper form. And --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I just want to -- to confirm that this is a true copy of Resolution 827 passed on the 25th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And this makes reference again to the establishment of an international Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for violations of international humanitarian law. And my question is: Do you recall what position the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia took with respect to the establishment of said Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
