utterances.text: While Bosnia and Herzegovina urged the establishment of this Tribunal, remember we met with significant opposition from the representatives of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be given an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do -- thank you so much. Thank you so much. It's admitted. What 65 ter number is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: 5001, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be exhibit number P2453, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could please go back to Exhibit P2439.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Which, for you, sir, was tab 10A, the first Mazowiecki report in the 1992 binder.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I apologise. I know it is cumbersome to have all these binders.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem at all. I certainly understand the significance of the Court's work here. I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 31 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: About two thirds of the way through the paragraph, it starts by talking about the fact that the leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia does not openly endorse the policy of ethnic cleansing. And then there's a sentence about two thirds of the way down that says: "However, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia clearly exercise very great influence on the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which without their cooperation would be completely cut off from the rest of the world." Was there any discussion at that time as to what the alleged cooperation was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Of course, from the level of military to the political, in particular, as you noted, this paragraph also speaks of the notion of cantonization. Actually as early -- as May of 1992 there's a reference in the Secretary-General's report that the policy of ethnic purification was being pursued in the context of a desire toward cantonization. So here we have speaking of military action that is in fact meant to bring about that result and meant to bring about ethnically pure cantons, and then such cantons being in effect realized through some political or negotiated process. That is being legitimatised through that process.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm finished with that document. I want to deal briefly with the second report that was released by the Special Rapporteur which you'll find at tab 10B and which has been marked as Exhibit 2440, Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you'd turn to --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Brief indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 of that report.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There, in that report, that paragraph begins by the sentence: "The Special Rapporteur shares the view of other observers that the principal objective of the military conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina is the establishment of ethnically homogenous regions. Ethnic cleansing does not appear to be the consequence of the war, but rather, its goal. This goal to a large accident has already been achieved through killings, beatings, rape, destruction of houses, and threats. Such practices have intensified in recent weeks, and there is less and less resistance on the part of the non-Serbian population, increasing numbers of whom are ready to abandon everything and to flee their home land. Recent events observed in the region of Prijedor, Doboj, and Kotor Varos prove that Serbian leaders in Bosnia and Herzegovina are not ready to desist in their plans." And then it continues on from there. I would like to know to what extent if any this statement in particular, this statement that "ethnic cleansing wasn't a consequence of the war but it's goal" was the subject of the discussion at the United Nations Security Council firstly in any private consultations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in fact a crucial point of discussion in the private discussions as well as public.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what action, if any, it spurred on the part of the United Nations Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Keeping in mind that the goal was ethnic homogenization of regions, of course, that would intend to also impact on the issue of what the solutions would be to the conflict. Of course, initially the entire point would be to discuss not only the fact that these crimes were occurring, but also that they were systematic with an intended goal. And then, of course, one would also have to discuss them in the context of the political solution to the conflict. Part of that political solution, in my view - that is, the view of the mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I believe in the view of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole, which, as I mentioned, had many members of -- of ethnic groups other than Muslim or Croat for that matter - was that these policies, since they were the objective, would have to be reversed as part of any political solution. And, therefore, that allowing people to return to their homes, rather than having them resettled, was the desired solution. During the discussions within the UN Security Council, the General Assembly, but particularly during negotiations, the Serbian side - and here I refer to both Belgrade and Pale - representatives, were in fact committed to preserving the status quo created by the conflict. That is, the consequences of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. Are aware of whether the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia received a copy of that report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As other reports, it would have been made available to them directly, that is, being forwarded to them as on the distribution list.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in terms of the discussions you've told us about taking place, you said both public and private with respect to the Security Council, do you recall to what extent, if any, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia participated in those discussions on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. In both -- at least at that time in the -- in the context of private discussions. I do not believe that at that moment the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Serbia and Montenegro spoke directly in a public forum of the UN Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. There is not obviously time to discuss each of these report, sir, so I'm going to turn to another topic. And going back chronologically now with events in 1992, I just want to turn to a couple of other developments. The first issue I just wish to establish is if you would look at tab 12 in the 1992 binder. It will be Prosecution Exhibit 471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's already in evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 471.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I'm there. Is this Resolution 781?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I'm interested, if you'd look at the numbered paragraphs on page 2 ...

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is a decision in paragraphs 1 and 2 I just wish to ask you about. The first paragraph indicates that there's to be established a ban on military flights in the air space of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that's not to apply to UNPROFOR flights. And the second paragraph: A request that the United Nations Protection Force monitor compliance with the ban on military flights, including the placement of observers where necessary at air fields in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. First, could you tell us what -- whether there was any particular event or events that spurned or caused the Security Council to pass this resolution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several. Number one, there were, of course, reports of military flights, and what I mean by that is it not only in the context of reinforcement of supplies but also in actual attacks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Originating from where?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Originating from what we believe is Serbia and Montenegro. And also this was -- this was a particularly intense --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- point of discussion at the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Unfortunately I was not quick enough on my feet. I object to the question unless there is personal knowledge with regard to where the flights were originating from. There is some indication of the basis of the knowledge. Otherwise, it's speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness to explain the context of the resolution which specifically mentions the placement of observers where necessary air fields in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. So I'm asking him to explain what information was available to the Security Council that resulted in them using that language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can also help on this point if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, there is an objection pending, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the question asked, that question -- that may well have been the Prosecutor's intent, but that question as it is framed does not indicate such an intent. And if that's the question being asked, then I have no objection at this time. But think -- once again, this is why I've been trying to get some kind of specificity and focus with regard to the questioning and the answer, otherwise, we're -- we really are running amock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, can you phrase the question as you have phrased it laterally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you recall then, sir, could you tell us what information the Security Council had available to it that caused it to use the language or to want to place observers at air fields in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, this question came -- this issue came in particular focus at that time because during the London Conference there was tremendous discussion of the violations of Bosnian air space by military flights. And in fact this was part of the negotiation -- discussions during the London Conference, which was -- which was attended by the Secretary-General and in his reports where these issues were addressed to the Security Council. And as a consequence of those discussions -- at the London Conference and the reports of the Secretary-General, then in fact this relation was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When was the London Conference?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the end of August 1992 [Realtime transcript read in error, "1993"]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- excuse me. They were independent reports before and after then but in fact these reports were very much addressed and if you would confirm during the discussions in the London Conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I just asked you -- but I have to interrupt. There's an error in the transcript, Your Honour, at line 16. The witness indicated "August 1992" and it reads "August 1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's noted, yeah, it should be 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And, sorry -- the London Conference was a meeting of whom, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a meeting called by the two primary negotiating bodies for the region, one is the United Nations, and the other one would be the Europe Union. And the London Conference was chaired by the prime minister of the United Kingdom, at the time, Mr. John Major and by the Secretary-General of the United Nations. It was also attended by representatives of the United States, the Organisation of the Islamic Conference. If I'm not mistaken, there were about 50 other countries besides the representatives of the countries in the region, including Serbia and Montenegro, that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as others.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And at the London Conference you indicated there was discussion of the violations of Bosnian air space by military. Was there any discussion of where the flights were originating?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. The information was at least some of the flights were originating from the territory of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If I could ask you to turn to tab 13 in that same binder. You should have before you document 65 ter 2189, Resolution 787.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Brief indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The resolution, looking at the second page midway through, notes -- there's a paragraph starting with: "Deeply concerned ..." and it says about reports of continuing violations of the embargo imposed by Resolution 713 and 724. And then the next paragraph expresses deep concern of reports of violations of the measures imposed by Resolution 757. We've already discussed those resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you remind us what Resolution 713 accomplished. If you know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Resolution 713 was an embargo upon -- what was then termed Yugoslavia in the territory of the former Yugoslavia of military goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the measures that were imposed by Resolution 757? What were we talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those actually now differentiated between Serbia and Montenegro that is the FRY, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and imposed sanctions upon the FRY for violations of the international border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, including, of course, violations of military goods and personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This resolution in paragraph 9 prohibits the transshipment --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- of a number of items, including -- and this is a transshipment through the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia -- crude oil, coal, iron, steel, et cetera, you can read what's before you. I want to know when this resolution was discussed what the reason was for including those particular materials.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This actually is in large part again borne out of the London Conference. During the London Conference under the leadership of Prime Minister Milan Panic, at that time. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Serbia and Montenegro had committed itself to numerous measures from refraining attacks on Bosnia and Herzegovina or at least having its territory used for such attacks from violations of that international border, in terms of men and goods, and, of course, from specific actions within Bosnia in terms of continuing attacks upon population centres. Unfortunately, those commitments were not heeded, and one would recall the Prime Minister Milan Panic soon challenged President Slobodan Milosevic for the Presidency of Serbia lost and resigned, and, of course, with the failure of those provisions of the London Conference meant to if not stop the conflict at least defuse it. This resolution in fact did come out. And it was meant to heighten the pressure upon Serbia to comply with those elements and to, of course, impose further sanctions for the fact that Serbia had not met those commitments.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't think you answered my question, sir, which was my why these particular materials were singled out?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they had military value.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was there any information available to the Security Council at that time to suggest, as you have indicated, that there had not been compliance on the part of the the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with the commitments that had been made at the London Conference?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The extent to which the questions are increasingly becoming leading and the Prosecution is testifying is becoming troublesome and if the witness wishes to testify that's fine. If the Prosecution wishes for the witness to testify, I would object on the grounds of it being leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. In respect of this question, I'm not leading. I think I'm following up on what the witness has already told us. I can rephrase if Your Honour wishes. I don't want to slow down any further, if you feel I should rephrase, I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think, yes -- sorry. I think the witness has testified to this fact. Failure to comply, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you answer the question then, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, is that all right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If that be the case then the witness is testifying, then I guess I would have another objection which would be asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: See, the witness has testified to the existence of failure to comply not to the extent ... oh, I see. If it has been answered. I don't know, I don't know what you're asking here for in addition to the fact that you comply. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My question is the witness has said that there was a failure on the part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to comply, and I'm now asking what evidence the Security Council had of that failure to comply with the commitments that it made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly wouldn't object to that question as propounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you are allowed, Madam Bolton, to put the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, my question then is: What evidence the Security Council had of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's failure to comply the time that this resolution was discussed, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the London Conference there was also a decision to deploy additional monitors on the border, and also from the existing UN Protection Force and other monitoring forces, in fact, that was the information that was being provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. Again, with respect to the next paragraph that resolution, paragraph 10, there's a special sanction that specifically relates to vessels operating from or in which there's a majority controlling interest in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. What was the information available to the Security Council at that time with respect to how vessels were being used by the federal -- or by -- how was this -- what was this contact?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without going into any sort of geography details here. There are lakes, there are water -- that is, there is sea and there is also rivers that in fact surround the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The border in particular between the FRY and Bosnia and Herzegovina is by river. And we were receiving information that particularly energy supplies were being delivered to the FRY and then we were also receiving information - we that is I should emphasise here for the Court' benefit that is not only the mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina but the Security Council was receiving information - that vessels were being used to transport goods across the river from Serbia and Montenegro into Bosnia and Herzegovina. These vessels would then presumably be able to avoid the monitors that were in most instances specifically focussed on the bridges across the river.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You said in your answer that you had information that particularly energy supplies were being delivered to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And then also such supplies being delivered as well as military supplies, that is, direct weapons and ammunition as well as men from the FRY to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. So, I'm sorry. Was the Security Council concerned about energy supplies being delivered to Yugoslavia as well weapons and ammunition coming from Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that those were in violation of Resolution 757.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does Resolution 757 prohibit any exports into FRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It -- it -- in fact, if those supplies are seen as part of the war effort within Bosnia and Herzegovina, it does, Your Honour. And this was -- this was a continuing point of discussion through the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure you have answered my question very directly. My question is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is: Did that resolution forbid any exports into Serbia itself, or did it forbid exports into Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a prohibition of the supply of goods to Serbia and Montenegro in that resolution, which in fact could include and did include under the -- there was -- Your Honour, to be very clear on this, the UN Security Council then would establish what was called a commission to review the sanctions regime. And this commission, of course, would, over time, deal with not only various new resolutions that would be meant to either amend or supplement previous resolutions, but they would also deal with the interpretation of whether or not certain resolutions were being violated. As an example, there was at various points in time a discussion whether flights over Bosnia and Herzegovina involving helicopters purely as supplies rather than being involved in attacks whether that was a violation of the no-fly zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- may I please, with respect, stop you. My question is very simply. Did Resolution 775, or 757 - I can't remember, prohibit the importation of supplies into Serbia and Montenegro. I think if you say yes or no then I would be happy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina understood it as yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this imports were allegedly coming from? Was it a worldwide embargo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The information was that the imports were coming from neighbouring countries, as well as over the international water-ways. That is the Adriatic Sea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I'm also asking: Was this a worldwide embargo imposed by the Security Council or by the UN?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And was it voluntary or mandatory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was under chapter 7 which means it was mandatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thanks. I will move on from here. Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You had started your answer by indicating that the intention was to put heightened pressure -- intention of this resolution was to place heightened tension or pressure on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. What was putting pressure on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia through the imposition of economic sanctions going to achieve?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, at this juncture, that would call for speculation on the part of this particular witness. He is being called as a fact witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I will reword.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In terms of the discussions that were taking place within the Security Council, either publicly or in informal consultations, what was putting economic pressure or heightened pressure on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia hope to achieve?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: By a denial of both goods that had economic value as well as military value, clearly the economy of Serbia and Montenegro would suffer. Those, of course, could include anything from a commercial goods to -- as we even discussed here, energy supplies. The idea would be of course that this would compel Serbia and Montenegro to comply with its earlier commitments now which numbered over several events starting with UN Security Council resolutions, and as I mentioned, the London Conference I believe up to this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia officially a party to this war at the time this sanction was imposed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well that may well call for a legal conclusion on the part of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What was position was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia taking as to whether it was part of the war at the time of this resolution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mission of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina certainly was of the view that --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Sir, -- I'm sorry, sir -- I have to cut you off. I'll interested in the position the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was taking as to whether it was a party to the war.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry I did not understand you. They, in fact, claimed not to be a party to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So within the context of the discussions that took place at the Security Council, what good was it going to do to impose economic sanctions on a country that wasn't part of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that question is certainly highly speculative and has been the subject matter of a myriad of tomes concerning the whole viability of sanctions, how to use sanctions, what is the appropriateness of them. This is certainly not an appropriate question for this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. The question is phrased within the context of the discussions that took place at the Security Council, I'm trying to get at if there were discussions about what good -- what -- what they were hoping to achieve by imposing the sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're asking it as a position by the FRY. Now he is not from the FRY. He is from Bosnia and Herzegovina. You can ask him about the position of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What did you, as Bosnia-Herzegovina, together with the Security Council, hope to achieve by what you did?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What I was actually trying to get, and my wording is perhaps incorrect, is -- and -- actually, I'm fine with the witness answering Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The view of Bosnia and Herzegovina was that greater pressure on Serbia and Montenegro, that is, the government in Belgrade, would bring about their withdrawal of direct and indirect support for the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was that strategy something that you shared with the Security Council at any time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And it was also something that we would share with the special commission, the sanctions committee of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how was that strategy received by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's -- no, it's okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I want to be very precise here. It was the Security Council I think who shared the same view or at least a very similar view. There may have been member states that were more hesitant as indicated in the vote of the Security Council, but the Security Council position, I think, was clear on this point. And these resolutions were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Just moving forward in time. Going to leave that resolution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Court's indulgence. If that could be marked as an exhibit number, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2454.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to the next document in that same tab, sir, for you, it is 65 ter 6765. It's -- it should be right behind the resolution we were just discussing.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And with respect to this document, all I want you to do is look at it and confirm for me whether it is a copy of an actual document released by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it, and it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be given an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be exhibit number P2455, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I want to move forward in time to 1993. And I would just ask to you if you can try to keep your answers to my questions as succinct as possible. Could you tell me what the state of peace negotiations or peace talks was at the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the Owen-Vance Plan, or -- I'm sorry, the Vance-Owen Plan is the more accurate description, and at that time it was about to be presented, and it was then to be -- continued to be discussed in New York.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And at that point in time, in terms of the territory of Eastern Bosnia, do you recall how much of the territory of Eastern Bosnia was in the control of the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Overwhelmingly with the exception of enclaves such as Srebrenica and Gorazde that held out. There were other enclaves as well which were soon overrun.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was happening then in the spring of 1993 in Eastern Bosnia, according to the reports that were being received?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to observe to that question as vague. By who? Who is receiving these report? Are we speaking about his delegation, are we speaking about the United Nations, are we talking about the Special Rapporteur? Are we discussing, for example, sanctions committee?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: According to the reports that were being received at the United Nations Security Council and General Assembly, what was happening in Eastern Bosnia in the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would define into two separate elements. One is ongoing military action that was meant to inflict direct harm. The second one is with the denial of necessities of live, including food. And at that point I was particularly involved because I had requested from the US Pentagon that they undertake air drops, which I do understand were undertaken at some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to turn to tab 15C in the binder for 1993. 65 ter numbers 8817, and it should be a document dated 5th April 1993. Do you have that document before you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And it purports to be signed by Muhamed Sacirbey. Can you confirm whether you did in fact author and sign this letter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What was your purpose in bringing to the attention the contents of this -- bringing to the attention the President of the Security Council the contents of this letter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Peace Plan at that time had been in fact rejected by the Serbian forces and the intensity of the attacks and denial of necessities of life had significantly intensified. Besides, of course, the very direct issues here that are addressed in terms of the military actions and the shelling. As -- as the focus of this area, of course, is the Drina river valley, again in particular Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The last sentence you write in document is: "May I request your kind assistance in circulating this letter as a document of the Security Council?" What does it mean if you ask a document to be circulated in that manner?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that it becomes an official document of the Security Council and then is circulated to all members of the council but also in fact all the United Nations member states, including, in this case, the FRY, Serbia and Montenegro delegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be given an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become exhibit number P2456, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: A brief indulgence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, was there ever an occasion when you asked that a document be circulated as a document of the Security Council when it wasn't circulated in that -- in that manner?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: One occasion. And that was very early on in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only aware of one occasion, and that was a particular point of discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: All others I'm quite aware that they were circulated. We confirmed that exactly because of that one situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Very briefly, that one document that wasn't circulated, what did -- what was the subject matter of that document so we can identify if for the record.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure we would have it in the record here, but it was a document relating to what we perceived as a re-definition of the conflict by some writing of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Approximately what -- can you tell us the month and year of that document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It occurred in late June or actually more like mid-June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. In the same tab that you were just in, there should be a second document with 65 ter number 4996, which is --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. It should be titled letter dated 15 April 1993 from the charge d'affaires of the permanent mission of Turkey; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And it starts by indication in the second paragraph that the only side that had not accepted the Vance-Owen Peace Plan up to that juncture was the Bosnian Serb side. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, yes, it is, keeping in mind my qualification about the use of the word Bosnian Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In the last paragraph there's talk of delay on the adoption of a draft resolution of the Security Council designed to strengthen sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you aware of -- first was there in fact a delay on the adoption of a draft resolution as described by the Turkish representative?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time as to why those -- the adoption had been delayed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what did you understand to be the reason for the delay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the presumed or the stated desire of Belgrade authorities to try to get the Pale Serbs to accept the Vance-Owen Plan. I should, of course, highlight at this point in time that we did not see any distinction between those two forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I was just looking at the clock, and it's time for the next recess. And we will come back to this issue after the break, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Sacirbey. Both yesterday and today we have been having some delays caused by the equipment. But if can you recall where we were before the break, we were discussing a letter authored by the Turkish representative. Do you still have that document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Is this a document that you received during 1993, or is this the first time you're seeing this document, or what's the situation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had -- no, this is a document that I had seen at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. He referred to a draft resolution, and I wonder if could you just briefly -- we are going return to this document. But if you can just return to the next tab in your binder. You should have 65 ter 5000?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is titled the draft resolution dated 8th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And can you tell whether or not this is the resolution that the Turkish representative was referring to as being a draft resolution to strengthen the sanctions and being delayed in adoption?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is, Ms. Bolton. As all of these document refer to draft resolutions which does not necessarily show the final form that they're adopted in, but I believe, actually, there is the one we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be given an exhibit number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's 5.000?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 5.000 is admitted as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2457, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if you could, sir, please, just flip back from the document from the Turkish representative being 65 ter 4996.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could just ask at this juncture that that be marked as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it be given an exhibit number too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become exhibit number P2458, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to turn to --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Should be 15E of the same binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I think you should have 65 ter 8818 in front of you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It should be a letter from --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the title of --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Letter dated 16 April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That -- it is a -- it is a Security Council resolution. So we'll try to see if we can identify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry. I think, then, if you would check tab F.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the -- is this the letter of 16 April from Muhamed Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I must have excellent hearing. I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Dealing with this document, sir, you refer -- and again the date is 16 April 1993. First paragraph, to the horrifying situation in Srebrenica that is so well documented by the media around the world and confirmed by the United Nations personnel on the ground. And then in the next paragraph you used the words "ongoing massacre." What information was the -- were you receiving as the Bosnia-Herzegovina representative as to what was unfolding in Srebrenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the United Nations force had sent in a military convoy to evaluate what was going on. I believe that was the convoy led by then-Commander General Morillon. And he in fact reported a very dramatic situation. And we did actually at that time also receive some television or video film if you would that showed that the population was being shelled. And what I mean by "shelled," there were many refugees in Srebrenica besides the residents of Srebrenica who were living in open areas so the shells that came in frequently hit -- population did not even have the benefit of being protected by walls. We also had firsthand evidence of some refugee, particularly children being evacuated by UN personnel, I believe, at that time, who had sustained difficult injuries some of which -- some of them which did not survive. And the question really was not what was going on. It was clearly a massacre inflicted mostly by heavy weapons, to some extent by sniper-fire, a population weakened by the humanitarian situation, but the question really was what to do about it, since in fact the UN force at least had -- apparently had a mandate to protect the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you talk about the information -- we started talking about what information had you available to you. To what extent was the information you've outlined made available to the United Nations Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain instances actually as strange as it may seem we were able to receive direct communication from some of these enclaves. That communication came either through satellite phone or through some other form of communication, actually came directly into our office. So we had information. Sometimes it came to us directly, sometimes came from the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina - that is, the government which I represented - and sometimes came in from the UN personnel on the ground. In all of those instances, I think we every endeavored and did convey that information in the form of UN documents whether it was a document to the president of the Security Council, or a document to the Secretary-General, which then was relayed to the entire membership.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So in this specific case, how much of the information you started off telling us about the television reports, the firsthand reports of refugees for example, how much of that information, if any, was made available or available -- was available, sorry, to the UN Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe all of it was. Although, of course, I received my information continuously, and that's the way it remains in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You indicated that General Morillon was involved in this incident, or this occurrence. Can you tell me what response the United Nations Security Council took to this situation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several sources of information coming in about General Morillon's presence. One, of course, was to the media; the other one was to the UN Secretariat; and the third one was actually through the representative of France to the Security Council, at that time Ambassador Jean Bernard Mery May. As far as I know, all or most of this information came into the UN Security Council through these three sources and was made available. At that time, these are very memorable moments, not only because of the horrific events unfolding, but we had a midnight sessions including one on -- over a weekend. And I remember on this occasion, but some others, well after midnight we were all, of course, not only waiting for what further information might come but also what in fact consensus might be reached either on a resolution or a presidential statement. Of course, UN Security Council resolutions did not have to be adopted by consensus, but it was desirable that especially in these situation there is would be a significant if not absolute consensus.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was there ultimately any kind of a resolution or a statement agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were several steps undertaken. Resolutions that in effect declared what was a relatively new concept declaring Srebrenica a safe area, and also from this was borne the mission of the UN Security Council team to actually visit Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that document we've been discussing could be marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2459.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you turn to the next tab in the binder you have before you, sir. You should have 65 ter 5003, and that is actually a report of the Security Council mission. Do you see that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm interested in pages 2 and 3. We only have reproduced the portions of the report, sir, that contain Resolution 819 from the Security Council. So --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- if you turn to page 2 of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. There's three aspects of this resolution I'm going to be asking you about, sir. First aspect I want to talk about, sir, is -- let me just read you a portion of the script, sir. It's page 3 at the top of the page in the English version. There's an indication that aware -- starts with the word: "Aware that a tragedy humanitarian emergency has already developed in Srebrenica and its surrounding areas as a direct consequence of the brutal actions of Bosnian Serb paramilitary units, forcing the large scale displacement of civilians, in particular women, children and the elderly." And then there are references in a text to three things. The first is a reference on the first page of the resolution, the paragraph that starts with the words: "Taking note." And that paragraph refer to the International Court of Justice in its order of 8th April 1993 in the case concerning application of the convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide. So I want to ask you about that case. Is that something that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As agent of Bosnia and Herzegovina, before the International Court of Justice on this case, I'm very familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Who were the parties to that action?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had brought action against the government of Serbia and Montenegro, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was the nature of the -- first, what were you alleging?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were alleging that in all the events, the horrific events that we have enumerated here - and I don't think the Court needs me go through those events - that these, in fact, did constitute not only systematic violations of international humanitarian law but in fact did constitute a breach of the convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What relief were you seeking from the Court, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first and most important step here which this paragraph refers to is provisional measures which would be a form of injunctive relief, i.e., the government in Belgrade should immediately cease and desist from all direct and indirect actions that in fact were part of the genocide. That meant, of course, military action directly involving the forces of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro, other forces, and, of course, all supplies and or political actions consistent with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How did you start this cause of action?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was initiated with a filing, if I'm not mistaken, in very late March, and we wished to make sure that in fact any peace agreement that might have been signed at that time, including the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, would not somehow estop the government but particularly the victims from pursuing remedies consistent with those remedies that victims of genocide would be entitled to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I would -- appreciating, of course, the Chamber's ruling with regard to answers that are given, I would appreciate it if the Prosecutor could kindly direct the witness to answer the questions asked as opposed to going off on relatively long discussions that are outside of the area. If the Prosecutor wishes to get those kinds of answers too, that should follow by way of question and answer as opposed to the narrative form as many of these questions have been taking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any, response, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect this question, I actually think the witness's answer was responsive to the question that was asked which was how the action started, and he told us when and that started with a filing in the Court. So I take my friend's point, and I have asked the witness to try to be as succinct as possible, and I'll remind him of that again. But I think that's as far as I can go, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You go a little further. You can stop him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll try, I find with the videolink it's hard.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: But we will continue on this note, sir. You talked about there being a filing and the letter refers -- sorry. You talked about there being a filing. I'm going suggest it was by way of an application to the court. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was service of your application or notice of your application in some form given to anyone from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, and the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did appear in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Who was -- who was responding on behalf of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I want to make sure I'm correct, though, in responding because there were several events before the Court. At that time it was their diplomatic representative in The Hague and also, if I'm not mistaken, representative of their Ministry of Justice. At some point in time, and I believe I cannot be precise on this, there was also outside counsel that was retained by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Whether he appeared actually on that date, I just -- for some reason I'm having a problem recalling that accurately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you look at tab -- the last -- well, I think it's tab 21 in my binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go to tab 21, what do you want to do with 5003?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to be coming back to the resolution, sir, so I'm not going to ask that we tender that yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you have before you -- should have before you a copy of document "International Court of Justice" is the first line, and it's 65 ter 6638.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. This is an order of 8 April 1993. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could direct you, please, sir, to paragraph 7 of the judgement -- or 7 of the order.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And that starts --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have it. It starts right at the very bottom of page -- is it -- it's not a page. I think it's -- it starts at the very bottom of --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The ERN number, Your Honours, here is 0342-3751.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: A brief indulgence. Just hold on. If you could just turn to the next page, sir. The 3242-3753 is the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We have a bunch of bullet points starting with one from the murder summary execution, et cetera. What are these bullet points referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, at this point I'm going object unless -- first of all, as best evidence. The document itself is the best evidence of what we referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, any comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't wish -- I'll try to be -- my friend is content, I guess, that it's -- that the document is authentic. If there is no issue with respect to that, then I can move on from this area of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly wouldn't take a position other than it's authentic. I wouldn't believe that the Prosecution would be submitting a filing that would be in front of an International Court of Justice if it was not authentic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could turn -- or I'll just direct you. I'll tell you, sir, that there is at paragraph 40 a reference to a -- a subsequent document entitle "A Supplementary Submission," which according to paragraph 40 included accounts of military and paramilitary activities, including the bombing and shelling of towns and villages, forced migration of civilians, allegations of executions, torture, rape. And my question is: That supplementary submission containing those accounts, in addition to being filed with the court, was a copy ever provided to the representatives of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was the source of the accounts or sources of the accounts that were included in that document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is this question within the personal knowledge of the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what the source or sources of the accounts that were included in that document were?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were both, as one might say, international sources, independent sources, as well as sources of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe, to be more accurate, I believe most of it in fact was independent sources or international sources as one would put. We -- we, I believe, also submitted some of the documents which we have referred to in the testimony today, including reports of Mr. Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia given an opportunity to respond to your application and materials?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was the nature of their response to your application? What position were they taking?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, once again, since we're dealing with a series of legal documents, the best evidence of the response would be the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But do we have the response in the document itself, or is the document filed by the plaintiff?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The document we have is the order, Your Honour. We don't have available to us the response, so I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, then, I mean, there's a problem because now the witness is being asked to interpret a legal document which is once again potentially outside of his ken, it's not what he was called --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He is not being asked to interpret a legal document. He is being asked to say what the response of the FRY was to the allegations that were put.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question was what was the nature of the response to your application, what position were they taking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, what position were they taking. Were they admitting or denying the facts, not the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm guided by the -- our guidelines, number 36, which deals with the best evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. The -- there is no documentary evidence of the response from the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. The best evidence of the response of the FRY is documentary evidence, which they have -- they have at this point chosen not to put forth. It is inappropriate for this witness to be discussing what their response is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The best --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can tell what you the response was. You can -- anybody in the world can tell what you the response was if they've read the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Now, the best evidence rule does say if the document is there, tender the document. If the document is not there, obviously the next best evidence is what we accept. That's what the rule says. And if there is no documentary evidence of their response and this witness is aware of the response, can he tell us. And if it is disputed, it is own to the Defence to dispute that response. Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us then what the response was of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to your application?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, was to challenge jurisdiction on several grounds, including succession issues; number 2, they, in fact, was a denial that they were a party to the conflict. In some instances there was -- in many instances there was a denial of the actual facts, and, if you would, allegations outlined therein. And in fact at one point in time the FRY did file a counteraction on behalf of what they claimed to be, quote/unquote, the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were you successful in obtaining the application you sought, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the provisional measures, we did obtain that. And there was a subsequent ruling. As to the eventual outcome of the ICJ case, there was a ruling issued in February of 2007, if I'm not mistaken, which did conclude that at least on some of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time that in fact genocide did occur. I'm not sure if I want me to go into any further detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to the document then that we have been discussing, 65 ter 6638, could I move for it to be admitted in evidence at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted, may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that being offered for notice again, or is that being offered for the proof -- for the truth of the matter of the allegations contained in the document? Now we have a legal pleading, and the purpose for which is being offered is of some moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's being offered for the purpose of the notice that it served us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Understanding its limitation, there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 6638 will become Exhibit P2460.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In that same tab, sir, right after the order that we've been discussing, you should find a one-page document, 65 ter 6638.02. It's a Security Council document with a date of 29th April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: 29th?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: 29th.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that there for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This was a letter addressed to the president of the Security Council from Boutros Boutros-Ghali. The text indicates they're transmitting the official text of the order. My question is: Once a document is sent to the president of the Security Council -- sorry. Let me just change my question. Was the -- was the order -- the subject of -- sorry -- discussion or circulation within the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I did ask a compounded question there. First, was it circulated?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. To whom?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was circulated once again, pursuant to the rules of documents being circulated, which is to all the members, including the FRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And in terms of the discussion that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Bolton, all the members of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the members of the United Nations including the FRY in view of its status at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By the United Nations, you mean the members of the General Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Members of the United Nations, okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a more difficult situation. That's a fair enough --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's just that -- the question had -- the question had said was it circulated to members of the Security Council, and now you say to all members of -- all members including the FRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If document 6638.02, if that could be marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2461.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We were discussing or you were indicating that the order was the subject of discussion in the Security Council. And can you tell us anything further in that regard? What was the impact on the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the most important element of this discussion would be how the Security Council in fact might have the order provisional measures to be enforced. Of course, and to some extent, they were self-enforcing, one would say, but in fact the Security Council itself could take further measures to ensure enforcement, including under chapter 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was the case raised in any other context outside of the United Nations -- sorry, was it raised with anyone from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia outside of the United Nations Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In what context was it raised?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was raised in the context of negotiations, and it was, of course, raised in the context of the actual, if you would, litigation itself. I'm sure that answer is not full. I'm sure that there were other areas, but those were two areas that I'm very much aware of. It was raised in the context of Dayton --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We'll come back to --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and all negotiations before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to Dayton at a later point in time. I want to return to Resolution 819 which was 65 ter 5000[sic]. Do you still have that available to you in the binder, sir, or do you need the tab number again?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just make sure. Yeah, I think we need the tab number, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think it's 15F.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you have the --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it the -- this is the delegation to Srebrenica, the Security Council delegation to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. And, sorry, I think we were looking at pages 2 and 3 of the document, and that's where I think you should find the text of the resolution, is that correct, or are you looking at a different document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe -- I believe I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. The second aspect of the order I wanted to discuss with you is numbered paragraph 3, which you'll find on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think we're now -- there's some -- are we talking about the -- the Registrar, and I are a little bit confused. I want to make sure -- are we talking about the report on Security Council mission established pursuant to Resolution 819 or are we speaking of something else, Ms. Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, we are talking about the report and we're looking at pages 2 and 3 of the actual report which reproduced the resolution.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that. And you're talking about point number ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Points number 3, numbered paragraph. The ERN on the page ...

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You've got that? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. It starts with: "Demands that ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. All right. So the wording there is -- this is the Security Council obviously: "Demands that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Serbia and Montenegro" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. Only for purposes of making sure that we have a correct record, this is 65 ter 5003, not 5000. 5000 is now an exhibit which is a the draft Resolution 819.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I thought I had said 5003, but I apologise if I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you did miss speak, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct it is 5003.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the paragraph we're dealing with reads as follows: "Security Council demands that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Serbia and Montenegro immediately cease the supply of military arms, equipment, and services to the Bosnian Serb paramilitary units in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." The Security Council included the word "cease" there. Do you recall what information the Security Council had available to it as to what military arms, equipment, or services had been provided up and to that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the information I think that we have already discussed, the delegation that we speak of here under the leadership of Ambassador Diego Arria had actually also visited Belgrade and in fact then provided some firsthand information related to this resolution. And number 2, it was also related to the decision, that is, the provisional measures of the International Court of Justice. I hope I'm being responsive to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't think you are, sir. My question, if I could repeat it for you, was: The Security Council demanded that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Serbia and Montenegro immediately cease the supply of military arms, equipments, and services. And my question was: What information, if you can recall, the Security Council had received up to that point in time as to what military arms, equipment, or services had already been provided.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to be just as complete about this answer.
