There is a sanctions committee at the Security Council that may provide information that I would not be privy to, but the other public information that has been made available to the Security Council would consist of all the reports and the letters filed by member states, including myself, and also the reports of the Secretary-General. There were reports of the Secretary-General that in fact indicated that there was still an ongoing flow of weapons and men. There were also letters written by member states also indicating that this had been occurring. There was also the report of this particular -- formal and informal report of this particular Security Council investigative body that was established just for the purpose of this trip, and then there was the information that was submitted to the International Court of Justice. I believe this provision is also responsive to that case or to that application to the International Court of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You mentioned the sanctions committee. What did the sanctions committee do? What was its job.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That question was clearly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is a question, clearly, that has been asked and answered previously. So the sanctions committee was discussed by this witness sometime ago, I believe, it our first section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give us a reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm trying to get there. I'm trying to get there. I got up because I didn't want to miss the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: While my friend's locating the reference, I just want to remind the witness not too speak quickly because the court reporter is transcribing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since I'm not finding it immediately, why don't we proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may put the question, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us what was the role was of the sanctions committee?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sanctions committee generally was led by one or more members of the Security Council, one of the permanent representatives on the Security Council. It -- it did have assistance of other staff or may have as the need required. Of course, it dealt with the -- with an issue that was rather fluid or dynamic at the time which was what in fact sanctions were being applied, how those sanctions were being defined, in terms of their breadth and depth, and, of course, any reports as to the violation of the sanctions. The work of the sanction committee was not necessarily in open meetings of the Security Council. Quite possibly it was at -- a part of the Security Council's work, but it was not in open session. And generally the sanctions committee might call upon the relevant representatives of member states, including myself, and/or the representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to provide either some insight or to answer some questions or potential allegations. I -- I frankly am not sure what kind of record consists of all the work of the sanctions committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Who actually would have drafted the resolutions that proposed sanctions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The drafting usually started with one or more countries who had a like view on the position. At that time, they might in fact engage other countries to become as we use the word "sponsors." But all the sponsors generally -- generally were members of the UN Security Council. Because the sponsorship might be limited let's say to three, four, five, six countries, it did not mean that reflected the support for the resolution. There would then be a separate vote where countries would say vote in favour, or would vote opposed, or would abstain. Of course, it was a P5 member, Permanent 5 member, then a vote against would in fact be a veto and the resolution would not be adopted. So all the resolution we have in front of us were adopted by majority with potential abstentions and votes against.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So you indicated there was a sanction committee that studied the sanctions and you told us what work they did. What would they do with -- you know, when they reached conclusions or had findings? What would happen to that information?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there could be some dispute or at least disagreement, lack of clarity, about what issues the resolution might affect. At that time, the sanctions committee might try to provide some clarity or might in fact ask the UN Security Council itself to provide some clarity. This was a very delicate and rather frequent task of the diplomatic officials at the United Nations. To deal with those that they understood to be involved in the work of the sanctions committee. But that's why I think we also do have so many elements -- so many times that the Security Council addressing sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What -- what I'm not understanding, sir, is you have a committee that is studying the issue of sanctions and then we have resolutions adopted that impose sanctions, and I'm trying to understand what role, if any, the sanctions committee has in the process of either -- of -- that results in the actual resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think there's a series of difficulties with the question posed, not the least of which is the witness has already informed us that information that -- that was created by the sanctions committee was, at times, given to the Security Council in his absence. So he -- I don't know whether he's really in a position foundationally to be able to speak to the question asked, since he was not a member of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, it must have missed me that point, that part of evidence. Can you ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What I'm trying to understand, sir, is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is the question that is being objected to. Mr. Guy-Smith says the witness told us that some of this information was given to the Security Council in his absence. I'm saying that bit of evidence missed my attention --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No. Sorry. Sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Perhaps we should locate the portion of the transcript because what I thought I understand the witness to say was that the Security Council was sometimes -- this committee was sometimes privy to information that he didn't -- he wasn't privy to. So we're -- I think we need to find the actual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Guy-Smith can help us where he said the Security Council decided in his absence. I don't know whether he said the Security Council or he said the committee. Some of this information was given to the Security Council in his absence. I'm saying that bit evidence missed my ... Yeah, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, if I might, I was taking my lead from page 88, line 22. I would like to be just as complete about this answer. "There is an sanctions committee at the Security Council that may provide information that I would not be privy to."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. So not -- not that he was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I -- the -- and then further, page 90 line 17: The work of the sanctions committee was not necessarily in open meetings of the Security Council." So I took the liberty of using the word "in his absence" predicated on those two particular assertions made by the witness. And if I was bold, in my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 90, line ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 17. And if I was bold in my assertion, I do apologise to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. Except that if you read that paragraph at line 17 he goes on to say: "Quite possibly it was at -- a part of the Security Council's work, but it was not in open session. And generally the sanctions committee might call upon the relevant representatives of member states, including myself, and/or the representative of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to provide either some insight or to some answer some questions or potential allegations." So there does seem to be sometimes when he is actually participating in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He may well be -- and perhaps we need clarification. That is what I understood based upon the answers that he has given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. But now we realize that at times he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that is it part of the difficulty that presents itself in the manner in which much of this testimony has been adduced because there is no date, no time, it expands a period of three years. So it leaves us in some what of a difficult position to make a determination of how to even test any of this information, let alone rely upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, and I do think that's too detailed to require a mind of a human being to remember, but if can he remember the issues that he discussed in this committee, on whatever date, he can tell us, can't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you know, I mean, there are many ways I can respond to that. Yes, he can. What memory does is a whole other issue, and I'm not going to have a discuss with you at this time. Certainly because of the lateness of the hour, because I don't think that would be profitable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Madam Bolton, to the extent that we have that prior answer to the -- that question, if you are able to solicit what you can solicit within the confines of the answer that he gave, you may do so. If you're not able to, you're not able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I think I want to go back to the answer he gave initially just for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we stop dead at 7.00 today.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We're stopping dead at 7.00 because Your Honour's been going all day, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So the question -- the original answer that you had given, sir, you indicated there was a sanctions committee at the Security Council that may provide information that I would not be privy to, but the other public information made available to the Security Council would consist of all the reports and letters filed, and then you continued on. I just wanted to make sure that I understand, when you're saying that the sanctions committee at the Security Council would provide information that you may not be privy to, who were they providing that information to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information would be received from the UN representatives on ground or other reliable sources that they feel they can rely upon, and the information then would be provided to the other members of the UN Security Council in preparation for votes on these types of resolutions or presidential statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to end questioning there for the day, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you end your questioning, ma'am, what do we do with 65 ter 5003?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We could tender it now. I will be coming back to it, but I don't know if it's possible -- I am going to be coming back to actual report at a later date, but as for this exhibit is it possible to just have the first pages 2, 3, and 4 filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would ask that we tender the entire report at this time because it is going to be a subject matter of some conversation. It makes more sense to have the entire report in under the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many pages is the report?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is no issue that the whole report will be put before you, it was just for clarification of the record. I think the whole report is -- I have to locate it, Your Honours. It's not that long, it is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I've got an answer. The report, 65 ter 5003 is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2462.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Sacirbey, I know I mentioned this to you yesterday. I'm duty-bound to mention it to you again. You are reminded that you may not talk to anybody during the time that the -- during the adjournment about the case, and until you are excused from testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now the case stands adjourned again until tomorrow, half past 2.00 in the afternoon, same venue, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
